title: Transient Art
strapline: Beautiful, arranged, and free to change forever.
intent: Because nothing is stuck down, transient art removes all fear of getting it wrong — children arrange, undo and rearrange endlessly.
Sorting, lining up and arranging loose parts is early pattern, symmetry and mathematical thinking made beautiful.
Composing with colour, shape and shine is pure creative decision-making, over and over.
The freedom to change it means children experiment far more boldly than with glue and paper.
It invites rich talk about choices, patterns and ideas — and about how an arrangement makes you feel.
implementation: Offer a beautiful, sorted collection of loose parts — buttons, pebbles, petals, gems, rings, shells, bottle tops — on trays or a mirror.
Present it invitingly (sorted by colour or type) so the materials themselves suggest arranging.
Sit and arrange alongside, without making a picture for children to copy.
Notice the mathematics: 'You've made a circle', 'That's a repeating pattern — red, blue, red, blue.'
Ask about choices and ideas: 'Tell me about your arrangement — what made you put those together?'
Offer frames, hoops, mirrors and light to compose within and around.
Photograph the finished arrangements so children can keep them even as they sweep them away to start again.
key_questions: Tell me about your arrangement — what made you choose those?
Can you see a pattern in what you've made?
What would happen if you turned it, or made it the same on both sides?
How does your arrangement make you feel?
What could you change to make it look different?

impact.text: Children arrange, undo and rearrange loose parts, making free creative choices without fear of mistakes.
Children make patterns, lines and symmetrical arrangements, exploring shape and space.
Children sort and group the materials by colour, shape and kind as they compose.
Children experiment boldly, trying arrangements and changing their minds freely.
Children talk about their choices, patterns and ideas, and how an arrangement makes them feel.
Children become deeply, calmly absorbed in composing and refining their work.

enhancements: A sorted collection of loose parts: buttons, pebbles, gems, shells, petals, bottle tops, curtain rings.
Mirrors, light panels and glass beads for shine and reflection.
Frames, hoops and trays to compose within.
Natural, seasonal materials — conkers, leaves, blossom — collected outdoors.
A camera or tablet so children can keep a photo of each arrangement.
Colour-sorted trays that make patterns and symmetry easy to reach for.

playing_exploring: Children explore and arrange freely, with no glue and no way to fail.
They test how the pieces look together, changing them as often as they like.
active_learning: Children become absorbed in composing, returning to refine an arrangement again and again.
creating_thinking: Children make and change patterns, plan compositions and explain the choices behind them.
